units.title: A storyboard is not a recorded shot
items: A frame is one still image. This is a storyboard illustration of a possible shot, not actual recorded footage.
A shot in a finished film is a continuous stretch of images between cuts. A take is an attempt to record that shot.
Several planned shots could be filmed and assembled into a scene.

story.title: One situation. Three possible story beats.
items: A person waits at a bus stop. The viewer sees where the action takes place.
A closer image of a clock could make waiting or an appointment feel relevant.
A closer planned shot could invite us to notice the person’s next choice or expression.

shot.title: How the image directs attention
items: A wider view places the person in their surroundings.
A closer view makes the person more prominent.
A detail shot can direct attention to an object, such as the clock.

editing.title: Choose what the audience learns first
items: The location becomes the viewer’s first information.
The clock may raise a question about time before we know the location.
The person becomes our first point of attention.

making.title: Start with a filmable idea
items: A single familiar location can be enough for a first exercise.
A small object can give an action meaning within the story.
Even a brief action can create a beginning, middle and end.

genres.title: One image could begin many genres
items: A person waiting at a bus stop might be part of a drama, comedy or mystery. The image alone does not decide the genre.
An illustrated clock could suggest an urgent appointment or could be a harmless detail.
A response can help viewers interpret the scene—but context still matters.

character.title: Want → obstacle → choice
items: Perhaps they want to catch a bus. This is a possible story setup, not a full screenplay.
A clock may suggest limited time if the wider story establishes an appointment.
Their decision, once performed, might reveal what matters to them.

dialogue.title: Words need a situation
items: Two strangers at a bus stop could speak politely or uncomfortably.
A character’s expression or movement can change the possible meaning of simple words.
An object can give the dialogue another layer of meaning if the scene establishes why it matters.

composition.title: Where do you guide attention?
items: A wide illustration provides information about the location and the person.
A closer view gives the person more visual prominence.
A detail illustration can call attention to a particular object.

shotlist.title: Plan pictures before recording
items: A wide view could establish where the scene happens.
You might plan to film a specific object if the story needs it.
You might also plan a view of the character. The final edit may use these in any order.
